title: Rank tests
objectives: Use the Wilcoxon and Mann-Whitney tests when returns are far from normal.

screens.title: Which strategy is better
screens.prose: Twelve days of daily returns, in %, for strategy A (blue) and strategy B (orange). Look at the dots before any numbers.
screens.question: On a typical day, which strategy does better?

options.text: A: most of its days sit to the right of most of B's

options.why: B's mean, 0.423%, is pulled up by one 6.5% day. On the other eleven days B mostly lost.
Eleven of B's twelve days sit below almost every A day.

hints.text: Ignore the far-right dot for a moment.
B's other eleven days run from $-0.40$ to 0.10.
A's days run from $-0.12$ to 0.48.

feedback.correct: A wins on a typical day; B's mean rests on one day.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare where most of each strategy's dots sit.

explain.text: The means say B: 0.423% against 0.185%, and Welch's $t = -0.4276$ ($p = 0.677$) leans B's way. One 6.5% day decides both. A test that looks at order, not size, sees what your eye saw.

screens.title: A rank cannot grow
screens.prose: Replace each return by its place in the pooled order of all 24 days: its **rank**. Drag B's big day left and right and watch its rank and B's mean.
screens.question: As you drag the big day from 6.5% down to 0.5%, what happens?

options.text: Its rank stays 24 while B's mean falls by half a point
Both its rank and B's mean fall steadily
options.why: The rank only changes when the day passes another day. Above 0.48 it stays the largest.
The mean moves with every bit of the drag: one day is a twelfth of it.

feedback.correct: The rank caps the day's influence: 24 is as big as it gets.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Watch the caption as you drag.

explain.text: From 6.5 down to 0.5, B's mean falls from 0.423% to $-0.077$%, but the day's rank stays 24. A **rank test** uses only the ranks, so one wild day counts as just the largest.

screens.title: Rank sums and U
screens.prose: Ranking the 24 days gives A a rank sum of 195. The **Mann-Whitney** statistic is $U_A = R_A - \frac{m(m + 1)}{2}$, the number of (A day, B day) pairs in which A's day is larger. $U_A + U_B = mn$.
screens.question: Fill in $U_A$ and $U_B$.

hints.text: $m = 12$, so subtract $12 \times 13/2 = 78$.

feedback.correct: $U_A = 117$ and $U_B = 27$: A wins 117 of the 144 pairs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract 78 from each rank sum.

byKey.r0c2: $U_A = 195 - 12 \times 13/2 = 117$. If you wrote 195, you skipped the subtraction.

explain.text: $U_A = 117$, $U_B = 27$. Counting all 2,704,156 ways to split the 24 ranks, the exact two-sided $p$ is 0.00829. The normal approximation with continuity correction gives 0.0102.

screens.title: What U measures
screens.prose: $U_A$ counts the pairs in which an A day beats a B day, out of $mn = 144$ pairs. So $U_A/(mn)$ estimates $P(X_A > X_B)$ for a random day of each.
screens.question: What is the chance that a random A day beats a random B day?

hints.text: Divide $U_A$ by the number of pairs.

feedback.correct: 81.25%: A beats B on a typical pairing four times in five.

byKey.b: That is $U_B/144$, the chance B wins.
byKey.ranks: You divided the rank sum by 300, the sum of all ranks. Use $U_A/(mn)$.

explain.text: $117/144 = 0.8125$. This is the probability a risk committee can read directly: on a typical day A beats B.

screens.title: Does it test the medians
screens.prose: A colleague says: "Mann-Whitney tests whether the two medians are equal." Consider strategy C with days $-1, -1, 0, 3, 3$ and D with $-3, -3, 0, 1, 1$.
screens.question: Both medians are 0. What does Mann-Whitney test, then?

options.text: Whether one distribution tends to sit above the other, $P(X > Y) \ne \tfrac12$
Whether the medians differ, so here it finds nothing
options.why: C beats D in 16.5 of 25 pairs (a tie counts a half). Equal medians do not make $P(C > D) = \tfrac12$.
It uses ranks only; the means play no part.

hints.text: Count the pairs where a C day beats a D day.
C's 3s beat every D day; D's $-3$s lose to every C day.

feedback.correct: It tests a tendency to sit higher, not the medians.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Equal medians can still differ in $P(X > Y)$.

byKey.median: You read it as a median test. It compares every pair of days, not two middle values.

explain.text: Here $U_C = 16.5$ of 25 pairs although both medians are 0. Only when the two distributions have the same shape does a shift in $P(X > Y)$ mean a shift in median.

screens.title: One strategy against zero
screens.prose: The **Wilcoxon signed-rank** test asks whether one strategy's days are centred above 0. Rank the absolute returns, then add the negative days' ranks: $W^-$. A has three losing days: $-0.08$, $-0.12$ and $-0.03$.
screens.question: What is $W^-$ for A?

widget.accept: 8: the three losses rank 3, 4 and 1 among A's absolute returns.
widget.label: W minus

hints.text: Sort A's absolute returns from smallest.
The losses have ranks 1, 3 and 4: $W^- = 8$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rank the absolute returns, then add the ranks of the negative days.

byKey.plus: That is $W^+$, the positive days' ranks.
byKey.count: That is the number of losing days, the sign test's count.

explain.text: $W^+ = 70$, $W^- = 8$, exact $p = 0.0122$ over the 4,096 sign patterns. B gives $p = 0.233$ (its $t$-test 0.461): its one big day cannot outvote eleven small losses.

screens.title: Back to the execution test
screens.prose: On lesson 9's 200 stock-days, three tests of B against A: the sign test gave 0.0194, the paired $t$ 0.00579. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the 200 differences gives 0.00484.
screens.question: Why is the sign test's $p$ the largest?

options.text: It throws away the sizes of the differences, so it has the least information
It is the wrong test for paired data
options.why: It is a valid paired test. It just ignores how big each difference is.

options.text: Fat tails make it lose power
options.why: Fat tails hurt the $t$-test, not the sign test; the sign test ignores sizes entirely.

hints.text: Look at the middle column.
The sign test keeps only whether each difference is negative.
Throwing away sizes throws away information.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what each test uses.

explain.text: The signed-rank test keeps the order of the sizes but not their values. So a few huge days cannot dominate. With fat tails ($t_4$ noise) it gives a slightly smaller $p$ here than the $t$-test.

screens.title: Ties and tiny samples
screens.prose: Rank tests need a rule for **ties**: tied values share the average of the ranks they span. Two days tied for ranks 5 and 6 each get 5.5. Small samples have few rank patterns: 3 against 3 has only $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ splits.
screens.question: With 3 days against 3, what is the smallest possible two-sided $p$-value?

widget.accept: 0.1: the two most extreme splits out of 20, $2/20$.
widget.label: Smallest p

feedback.correct: $2/20 = 0.1$: no 3-against-3 result can be significant at 5%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Two of the 20 splits are as extreme as possible.

byKey.one: That is one-sided, $1/20$. Two-sided counts both extremes.

explain.text: All three A days on top, or all three at the bottom: 2 of 20 equally likely splits. So $p \ge 0.1$ whatever the data.

screens.title: U and its exact p in code
screens.prose: Compute $U$ with `scipy.stats.rankdata`, which averages ties. Then the exact null distribution of $U$. Walk up the pooled ranks, counting the ways to give $k$ of them to $a$ for each total $U$.
screens.question: Complete `rank_sum_u` and `mw_exact_p`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import rankdata


def rank_sum_u(a, b):
    """U for sample a, with average ranks for ties."""
    ...


def mw_exact_p(a, b):
    """Exact two-sided Mann-Whitney p for small samples without ties."""
    ...
widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import rankdata


def rank_sum_u(a, b):
    r = rankdata(np.r_[a, b])
    m = len(a)
    return float(r[:m].sum() - m * (m + 1) / 2)


def mw_exact_p(a, b):
    m, n = len(a), len(b)
    # ways[k][u]: ways for k of the first i ranks to be a's with U-count u
    from math import comb
    f = np.zeros((m + 1, m * n + 1))
    f[0, 0] = 1
    for i in range(m + n):
        g = f.copy()
        for k in range(1, m + 1):
            # rank i + 1 goes to a: it beats the (i - (k - 1)) b values below it
            beat = i - (k - 1)
            if 0 <= beat <= n:
                g[k, beat:] += f[k - 1, :m * n + 1 - beat]
        f = g
    dist = f[m] / comb(m + n, m)
    u = rank_sum_u(a, b)
    lo = min(u, m * n - u)
    p = 2 * dist[:int(lo) + 1].sum()
    return float(min(1.0, p))
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Three check $U$, including a case with ties. Three check exact $p$-values against `mannwhitneyu(..., method='exact')` in Pyodide: 0.008293 for the strategies. Each runs in well under a second. The first run loads NumPy and SciPy, about 10 seconds.

hints.text: `rankdata(np.r_[a, b])`, then the first `len(a)` ranks.
In the count, giving the next rank to $a$ adds the number of $b$ ranks already placed to $U$.
Two-sided: double the lower tail at $\min(U, mn - U)$, capped at 1.

feedback.correct: $U = 117$ and the exact $p = 0.008293$, as scipy says.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check the tie rule and the doubling of the tail.

explain.text: The count is a dynamic programme over ranks: 2,704,156 splits never have to be listed. Ties change the null, so this exact count is right only for untied data.

screens.title: Which wins on a typical day
screens.prose: A risk committee compares two strategies' daily P&L over a quarter. Strategy B's mean is higher, entirely because of one day it caught a takeover.
screens.question: What should the committee be told?

options.text: B's mean is higher, but A wins on a typical day: $P(A > B) = 0.81$, Mann-Whitney $p = 0.008$
B is better: its mean is higher
options.why: The mean answers "which made more in total", and that rests on one day.

options.text: Drop B's big day and compare means
options.why: Dropping a day after seeing it is a choice made from the result. The rank test needs no such choice.
The $t$-test is swamped by one day's variance; the ranks show a clear pattern.

hints.text: Two different questions: total P&L, or a typical day.
The rank test answers the typical day.
Report both, with $P(A > B)$.

feedback.correct: Two questions, two answers, both reported.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Separate the total from the typical day.

byKey.drop: You dropped the day by hand. A rank test downweights it by a rule fixed in advance.

explain.text: The mean asks about the total, which one takeover day decided. The rank test asks which strategy wins on a typical day, often the committee's real question.

ideas: Ranks cap a wild day's influence: B's 6.5% day counts as rank 24 and no more.
Mann-Whitney's $U_A$ counts the pairs A wins; $U_A/(mn) = 0.8125$ estimates $P(A > B)$, and $p = 0.00829$.
Wilcoxon's signed-rank test centres one sample on 0; it uses more than the sign test and less than the $t$-test.

formula.name: Mann-Whitney
formula.note: Ties take average ranks; tiny samples cannot reach small $p$.

summary.trap: Mann-Whitney is not a test of medians: it tests whether one distribution tends to sit above the other.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ties share the average of the ranks they span.

byKey.three: You gave both the lower rank.
byKey.four: You gave both the upper rank.

explain.text: The two tied values occupy places 3 and 4, so each gets 3.5; the rank sum is unchanged.

quiz.prose: An analyst sees B's 6.5% day, deletes it, and runs a $t$-test on the rest: B now looks clearly worse.
quiz.question: What is the problem?

options.text: The deletion was chosen after seeing the data, so the $p$-value no longer means what it says
None: the day was an outlier
options.why: It may be a real day. Choosing what to delete from the result biases the test.

options.text: Only that the sample shrinks to 23 days
options.why: The smaller sample is the least of it; the choice itself is the problem.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask when the rule was chosen.

explain.text: A rank test fixes its treatment of extremes in advance. Deleting by eye after seeing the result is a forking path.

quiz.prose: Two samples of 10 days each give $U_X = 70$.
quiz.question: What is the estimated chance that a random X day beats a random Y day?

byKey.y: That is the chance Y wins.
